t.3.24.1: Having arrived at the hermitage together with his vanguard, Khara saw Rāma, the slayer of foes, standing enraged with his bow held firm.
t.3.24.3: At Khara's command, the charioteer urged on the horses toward the place where mighty-armed Rāma stood alone, shaking his bow.
t.3.24.2: Seeing him, he raised his strung bow with its harsh twang and urged the charioteer, saying, “Let the chariot be driven on to face Rāma.”
t.3.24.4: Seeing him rushing forth, all those night-roaming ministers, roaring a mighty roar, surrounded him.
t.3.24.5: Khara, delighting as he went into the midst of those Yātudhānas, appeared like the red planet Lohitāṅga risen in the midst of the stars.
t.3.24.6: Then all the night-roaming demons, enraged, showered with weapons of many kinds that Rāma of the fearsome bow, who was hard to conquer.
t.3.24.7: With iron clubs, spears, lances, swords and battle-axes, the Rākṣasas, intent on their fury, struck Rāma in battle.
t.3.24.8: Those mighty ones, resembling storm clouds and roaring loudly, rushed in battle at Rāma Kākutstha, eager to slay him.
t.3.24.9: Those hosts of rākṣasas loosed showers of arrows upon Rāma, like rain clouds pouring down torrents upon the lord of mountains.
t.3.24.10: Surrounded by those terrible hosts of Rākṣasas, Rāghava looked like Mahādeva encircled by the hosts of his attendants on the lunar days sacred to him.
t.3.24.11: Those weapons loosed by the Yātudhānas Rāghava received with his arrows, as the ocean receives the floods of rivers.
t.3.24.12: Though his limbs were pierced by those dreadful weapons, Rāma did not waver, like a great mountain struck by many blazing thunderbolts.
t.3.24.13: Pierced and smeared with blood on all his limbs, Rāma, the Rāghava, looked like the sun enveloped by the clouds of twilight.
t.3.24.15: Then Rāma, greatly enraged, drawing his bow into a full circle, loosed sharpened arrows by the hundreds and then by the thousands.
t.3.24.14: The gods and Gandharvas, the Siddhas and the supreme seers grew despondent when they then saw him, standing alone, surrounded by many thousands.
t.3.24.16: In battle Rāma playfully loosed heron-feathered arrows that flew straight, hard to ward off and hard to endure, like the noose of Kāla.
t.3.24.17: Those arrows, released by Rāma with playful ease among the enemy hosts, took away the lives of the Rākṣasas like nooses fashioned by Kāla.
t.3.24.18: Having pierced through the bodies of those Rākṣasas, those arrows, drenched in blood, shone as they passed into the sky, possessing a splendor equal to that of a blazing fire.
t.3.24.19: Countless arrows of Rāma, exceedingly fierce and carrying off the life-breaths of the rākṣasas, flew forth from the circle of his bow.
t.3.24.21: Then, being pierced by nālīka and nārāca arrows and by sharp-pointed vikarṇi shafts, the night-roaming rākṣasas raised a terrible cry of anguish.
t.3.24.20: With those arrows he struck down bows, the tops of banners, armour and heads, and many thighs like elephants' trunks, together with hands and ornaments.
t.3.24.22: That army, tormented by Rāma with sharp arrows that pierced the vital parts, found no relief, like a dry forest ravaged by fire.
t.3.24.23: Some night-roaming demons, valiant and of terrible strength, filled with supreme fury, hurled spears, swords and battle-axes at Rāma.
t.3.24.24: Warding off those weapons with his arrows, the mighty-armed Rāghava took their lives in battle and severed their necks.
t.3.24.25: And those night-wanderers who remained there, dejected and tormented by arrows, ran to Khara alone for refuge.
t.3.24.26: Taking them all up again and reassuring them, Dūṣaṇa, enraged, rushed at Kākutstha, as Antaka might rush at Rudra.
t.3.24.27: But they all turned back again, made fearless by having Dūṣaṇa as their refuge, and rushed at Rāma himself, armed with sāla trees, palms and rocks.
t.3.24.28: Then there arose a wondrous battle, tumultuous and hair-raising, exceedingly terrible, between this Rāma and those rākṣasas once more.
